lead: Whether a fiber is single-mode is not fixed by the fiber alone: it depends on the wavelength used. The V number compares the core size with the wavelength, and a step-index fiber carries only one mode while V < 2.405. The wavelength at which V equals 2.405 is the cutoff wavelength: longer wavelengths give single-mode operation, shorter ones give several modes. This one inequality decides whether a link can use a cheap LED and multimode fiber over a few hundred metres, or needs a laser and single-mode fiber over tens of kilometres.
prereq: You need: the V number from Step-index and graded-index fibers.

sections.h3: LP modes and the single-mode condition

blocks.text: In communication fibers n₁ and n₂ differ by well under 1 %, so the fiber is weakly guiding and its exact modes group into nearly degenerate sets called linearly polarized (LP) modes, labelled LPlm. Each LP mode has its own cutoff value of V, set by zeros of Bessel functions.
So a step-index fiber is single-mode when

blocks.where: a is the core radius, λ the vacuum wavelength (same unit), NA = √(n₁² − n₂²).

blocks.text: Below 2.405 only LP₀₁ travels, in two polarizations. Single-mode does not mean the light runs in one straight ray; it means the field has one fixed shape across the core. With large V the fiber is multimode and carries about V²/2 modes.
Set V = 2.405 and solve for λ. The result is the cutoff wavelength λc, the shortest wavelength at which the fiber is single-mode:

blocks.where: λ<sub>c</sub> has the unit of a. Since V = 2.405 λ<sub>c</sub>/λ, the fiber is single-mode for λ > λ<sub>c</sub> (V < 2.405) and multimode for λ < λ<sub>c</sub> (V > 2.405).

blocks.text: Take a = 4 µm and NA = 0.11. Then 2πa·NA = 2.765 µm and λ<sub>c</sub> = 2.765/2.405 = 1.150 µm. At 1.31 µm, V = 2.765/1.31 = 2.11 (single-mode); at 1.55 µm, V = 1.78 (single-mode); at 0.85 µm, V = 3.25, so LP₁₁ also travels and the fiber is multimode there.

Designers place λ<sub>c</sub> below the shortest working wavelength with some margin. Standard single-mode fiber is specified with a cabled cutoff of at most 1260 nm, so both the 1310 nm and 1550 nm windows are single-mode. The cutoff should not be pushed far below the window, though: a small V means a weakly held mode that is lost easily at bends.

sections.h3: Mode field diameter and choosing a fiber

blocks.text: The LP₀₁ field is close to a Gaussian and reaches into the cladding. The mode field diameter (MFD) is the diameter at which its intensity falls to 1/e² of the peak. For standard single-mode fiber it is about 9 µm at 1310 nm and about 10 µm at 1550 nm, larger than the 8 to 9 µm core, and it grows as V falls. MFD, not the core diameter, sets splice loss between fibers and the coupling from a laser.

With one mode there is no intermodal dispersion, so single-mode fiber carries the highest bit rates over the longest spans; the price is a laser source and tight alignment of a core only about 9 µm wide. Multimode fiber (V in the tens) accepts light from LEDs and VCSELs and uses cheap connectors, but its many modes spread pulses, so it serves links of a few hundred metres. When several modes arrive together at a receiver, the speckle pattern they make shifts with vibration and temperature, adding modal noise.

examples.question: A step-index fiber has core radius a = 4.0 µm and NA = 0.11. (a) Find its cutoff wavelength. (b) Is it single-mode at 1.31 µm? Support the answer with V.
steps: 2.110 < 2.405, so only LP₀₁ is guided. Equivalently, 1.31 µm is longer than λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.150 µm.
examples.answer: λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.15 µm; at 1.31 µm V = 2.11 < 2.405, so the fiber is single-mode.

examples.question: Design: a single-mode fiber is to have n₁ = 1.48 and Δ = 0.003, and its cutoff must not exceed 1.26 µm. Find NA, the largest core radius allowed, and, for a = 4.1 µm, the cutoff and V at 1.31 µm and 1.55 µm.
steps: With a = 4.1 µm: 2πa·NA = 2π × 4.1 × 0.1146 = 2.953 µm, so λ<sub>c</sub> = 2.953/2.405 = 1.228 µm, inside the limit.
Check: λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.228 µm is below 1.31 µm, so both windows are single-mode, as the V values say.
examples.answer: NA = 0.115 and a must not exceed 4.21 µm; with a = 4.1 µm the cutoff is 1.23 µm and V is 2.25 at 1.31 µm and 1.91 at 1.55 µm.

traps: Single-mode needs λ longer than λ<sub>c</sub>. A wavelength shorter than cutoff makes V larger than 2.405 and the fiber multimode.
2.405 is the LP₁₁ cutoff (first zero of J₀). LP₀₁ has no cutoff, so a fiber never guides zero modes.
V is dimensionless and uses the radius a. Writing V in µm, or using the diameter, is a common slip.
λ<sub>c</sub> depends only on a and NA, not on power, fiber length or connectors.
A fiber 'single-mode at 1310 nm' has λ<sub>c</sub> below 1310 nm, not equal to it.

quiz.q: Write V for a step-index fiber and the single-mode condition.
quiz.a: V = (2πa/λ)·NA with a the core radius; single-mode when V < 2.405.
The diameter at which the intensity of the fundamental LP₀₁ mode falls to 1/e² of its peak; it is larger than the core and sets splice and coupling loss.

quiz.q: Why does V fall when the wavelength rises, and what happens to the modes?
quiz.a: V is proportional to a/λ, so a longer wavelength makes the core look smaller. The mode count (about V²/2) falls, and once V drops below 2.405 only LP₀₁ remains.

quiz.q: A step-index fiber has a = 5.0 µm and NA = 0.20. Find λ<sub>c</sub>. Is it single-mode at 1.55 µm?
quiz.a: 2πa·NA = 6.283 µm; λ<sub>c</sub> = 6.283/2.405 = 2.61 µm. At 1.55 µm, V = 6.283/1.55 = 4.05 > 2.405 (even above 3.832), so it is multimode.

quiz.q: A fiber has cutoff 1.20 µm. Find V at 0.85 µm and at 1.55 µm without knowing a or NA.
quiz.a: V = 2.405 λ<sub>c</sub>/λ: at 0.85 µm, V = 2.405 × 1.20/0.85 = 3.40 (multimode, LP₁₁ guided); at 1.55 µm, V = 2.405 × 1.20/1.55 = 1.86 (single-mode).

quiz.q: Two fibers have NA = 0.11 and core radii 4 µm and 8 µm. Compare them at 1.31 µm.
quiz.a: 4 µm: λ<sub>c</sub> = 1.15 µm, V = 2.11, single-mode. 8 µm: λ<sub>c</sub> = 2.30 µm, V = 4.22, which is above 3.832, so LP₀₁, LP₁₁, LP₂₁ and LP₀₂ all travel: multimode.

quiz.q: Why is single-mode fiber used for long-haul links even though it is harder to handle?
quiz.a: With one mode there is no intermodal dispersion, so pulses stay narrow over tens of kilometres and high bit rates are possible in the low-loss 1550 nm window. The small core needs lasers and precise splicing, but over a long span that cost is far smaller than adding regenerators.

beyond: Not for the exam. Standard single-mode fiber follows ITU-T G.652, and bend-insensitive fiber for buildings follows G.657, which keeps the mode well held at tight bends. Few-mode fiber deliberately carries a handful of modes so that each can carry its own data, separated again by MIMO signal processing. Hollow-core fibers guide light mostly in air for lower latency. Search next for effective cutoff measurement, bend-insensitive fiber and few-mode fiber.
